newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FEATURE - Reforging the chocoholic's grail, Venezuelan cacao.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Reforging the chocoholic's grail, Venezuelan cacao.

text.p: Along a wild stretch of Caribbean coast, a handful of plucky financiers with an epicurean bent seek the chocoholics' holy grail: the Venezuelan cacao bean.

Although it is a pale shadow of its former glory, when Venezuela's famed criollo species was its largest export, aficionados still drool over this Rolls Royce of chocolate, whose subtle aroma and almost narcotic afterglow are unique in the chocolate world.

"I gave some to a buyer who had spent a lifetime in the business and he said he'd never tasted anything like it," local connoisseur and broker John Kehoe enthused. He is one of a handful of entrepreneurs seeking to market the royal bean and restore its dented prestige on the back of its famed ability to tickle the pleasure centres of the brain.

In the small colonial village of Chuao, accessible only by sea although a mere 25 miles (40 km) from Caracas, historian Franciso Planchez evokes the days of Venezuelan gourmet fame, before artificial flavoring. "French and Swiss chocolatiers occasionally pass through here on buying trips," he said, raking his fingers through a tray of Chuao's dark beans, which still enjoy a near mythic reputation among connoisseurs, like Cuban cigars or French wine.
"But this is an extractive mining country now ... we've lost the memory," he added as a voluptuous, almost narcotic aroma ballooned from under his hand.
A TASTE OF THE PAST

Venezuelan cacao -- cocoa as Anglo-Saxons better know it -- was a source of great wealth when oil was nothing more than "Devil's excrement," as the Spaniards called it. Venezuelan chocolate barons were known as "Gran Cacaos" -- "Big Pods" -- and Chuao's Gran Cacao was one of the biggest pods of all.
"Then came oil," Planchez said.

Venezuela's first derricks went up in the 1940s. By the 1970s petro-dollars were raining down. Venezuelans left the countryside to work in booming new towns, agrarian reform broke up large estates, and state marketing board Funcacao fixed prices and cross-bred the royal criollo bean with lesser species, reducing quality.
"I must admit, the old Funcacao was corrupt," said its new director, Jose Antonio Gonzalez, who presides over a vastly diminished office from a poky Caracas office.

Cacao production slumped from 20,000 tonnes in the 1960s to 15,000 today. And for the 15,000 producers who grow much of the country's crop on small plots, the glistening pods, the size of small footballs, are still split by machete. The tightly packed beans are shucked from the tangy white flesh by hand, left briefly to ferment in wooden vats, sun-dried on hot open patios and then sent to market.

Exporters say competitive buying has improved farmers' prices since Funcacao's monopoly status was revoked in 1991. The board's demise also opened the way for private growers such as Caracas-based financier Kai Rosenberg.
GRAN CACAOS TO THE RESCUE
In one of Chuao's neighbouring coastal valleys, a middle-aged but trim Rosenberg, riding crop in hand and clad in tan jodhpurs, swaggered through a recently acquired plantation chomping on a cigar.

Brilliant crimson, yellow and green cacao pods jut from low branches on thick short stems like wax fruit, weeds have been cleared and a sinuous irrigation channel burbles among shade trees as in a fairy tale forest.

"In five years, I'd like to be able to tell you: I produce the best in the world," he said. He hopes to join other local firms that have recently signed joint ventures with foreign chocolatiers such as France's prestigious Valrhona.

Family-run Chocolate del Rey now exports a hybrid criollo bean, Carenero Superior, as a dark, heady chocolate. There are plans to award appellation status, like vineyards, to cacao's once royal names -- Chuao, Porcelana, Barlovento -- but such modern notions percolate slowly into the country's backwaters.

Chuao's once proud hacienda has crumbled, its decay reflecting a wider history of opulence and grandeur slowly faded to waste and neglect. The 490-acre (200 hectare) cooperative is still farmed with pride by the few hundred descendants of the slave families that always lived there, but it never quite turns a profit.

Kehoe said Chuao's productivity could be more than four times the low national average, the plantation could produce 100 tonnes per year rather than the 20-odd it now does, and the beans could carry an $800 premium over more lowly origins.
But some wonder if this will ever come to pass. Walled in by mountains and a sea rich with fish, Chuao's generous nature muffles the hard commercial sounds of the outside world.
"Nothing will happen here, nothing will change," mused Planchez as he strolled across the town square in the shade of its 18th century church. "Why should it?"
